name: Fractional CO2 laser (CO2RE, UltraPulse, SmartXide)
lead: Fractional CO2 laser resurfacing uses a 10,600 nm carbon dioxide laser, invented by C. Kumar N. Patel at Bell Labs in 1964 [1], in a fractional pattern that vaporizes microscopic columns of skin while leaving tissue between them intact. Commercial systems include CO2RE, UltraPulse and SmartXide.

It is used in dermatology for acne scars, wrinkles, burn and surgical scars, and other conditions; published studies include burn-scar cohorts, acne scar studies in Asian patients and randomized trials combined with other therapies [2][3][4][5]. Wikipedia notes that CO2 resurfacing carries higher risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than erbium lasers [6]. The same device class has also been studied for vaginal atrophy, outside the appearance focus of this wiki [7][8].
infobox: 1964, C. Kumar N. Patel, Bell Labs [1]

paras: A large prospective before-and-after cohort reported remodeling of hypertrophic burn scars with long-term follow-up [3]. A randomized split-face study combined adipose stem cell exosomes with fractional CO2 laser for acne scars [4], and a randomized trial used fractional CO2 laser to intensify photodynamic therapy of actinic keratoses [9]. A review covers the role of CO2 and fractional CO2 lasers in dermatology [5].

Wikipedia states that CO2 resurfacing produces more heat than erbium lasers and so carries a higher risk of hypopigmentation and scarring; other reported complications include hyperpigmentation, acne and herpes outbreaks [6]. Downtime is longer than for non-ablative fractional lasers.

Controlled and cohort studies exist for scars [3], acne scars [4], and actinic keratosis [9]. Registered trials include acne scars in Asians (n=12) [10], cesarean-section scars [11], cleft-lip scars (n=120) [12] and melasma with topical agents [13]. Studies on vulvovaginal atrophy include a randomized trial against topical estriol [7] and pilot studies [8], noted here only as related uses of the device category.

timeline.event: CO2 laser invented by C. Kumar N. Patel at Bell Labs [1].

card.summary: The heavy-duty fractional laser for scars and deep wrinkles: best-studied, more downtime and risk than gentle lasers.
card.note: Higher risk of pigment loss and scarring than erbium lasers.

quick.overview:
Fractional CO2 lasers vaporize tiny columns of skin to resurface scars, wrinkles and photodamage. They are among the more intensive options in laser resurfacing.

Published support includes cohort studies and randomized trials, mainly for scars.
quick.mechanism: The 10,600 nm beam is absorbed by water in tissue, ablating microscopic channels and triggering collagen remodeling; untreated skin between channels speeds healing.
quick.risks: Reported risks include hypopigmentation, hyperpigmentation, scarring, acne and herpes outbreaks [6]. Recovery is typically longer than for non-ablative lasers.
